title: Friction Stir Welding Process and Cryogenic Mechanical Properties of 2219 Aluminum Alloy Thick Welded Blanks
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: To prepare reliable thick aluminum alloy tailor welded blanks for cryogenic forming, 2219 aluminum alloy friction tailor welded blanks that has the thickness of 12 mm were selected as the research object in our study. Vickers hardness tests were employed to clarify the property distribution across the weld cross-section. Room temperature uniaxial tensile tests have been used to reveal through- thickness deformation behavior under tensile loading. The mechanical tests at room and cryogenic temperatures were employed to investigate the effects of welding parameters of the friction tailor welded blanks on the mechanical properties, and evaluate the cryogenic formability of the welded blanks. Results show that the single-sided FSW specimens exhibit decreased hardness values from the top to the bottom surface, causing more severe deformation in bottom region and macroscopic bending under tension stress condition. In contrast, the double-sided FSW specimens exhibit a more uniform hardness distribution across the weld cross-section, resulting in nearly symmetric deformation and no significant bending. Lower welding speeds combined with higher rotational speeds significantly improved the ductility of the tailor welded blanks. The optimal welding parameters are identified as 200 mm/min and 800 rpm, showing a 321.1 MPa tensile strength and a 22.2% elongation, at room temperature after water quenching and solution treatment. title: A Study on the Tribological Behavior of Silicon Nitride-Based Multiphase Ceramics Under Different Lubrication Systems
journal: SAE technical papers on CD-ROM/SAE technical paper series
abstract: To address the urgent need for high-performance self-lubricating ceramic materials for rolling bearings under high-speed operating conditions in the aerospace sector, this study employs Si3N4 as the matrix and incorporates nano lignin and graphene nanoplatelets (GNPs) to develop a self-lubricating composite ceramic system. This paper systematically studies the tribological characteristics and wear mechanisms of the composites. The results indicate that nano lignin undergoes pyrolysis during sintering, forming nitrogen-doped graphene quantum dots (N-GQDs). These structures are uniformly distributed at grain boundaries and participate in the formation of a lubricating film during the friction process, thereby significantly improving the material’s friction and wear properties. Under the special conditions (10 N, 1000 r/min), the composite material exhibited optimal tribological performance when the nano-lignin content was 2 wt.%, The friction coefficient decreased to 0.22 and a significant decrease in wear rate, demonstrating excellent friction- reducing and wear-resistant effects. In contrast, the introduction of GNPs failed to effectively improve friction performance, which may be attributed to their poor dispersion in the matrix and weak interfacial bonding. title: Cyclical Force Generation for Triboelectric Nanogenerators: A Review of Mechatronic Approaches, Challenges and Future Perspectives
journal: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Abstract Triboelectric nanogenerators (TENGs) convert low-frequency and irregular mechanical energy into electrical energy for self-powered sensors, wearable electronics, Internet-of-Things devices and distributed energy systems. Although major advances have been made in triboelectric materials, surface engineering and device architectures, the mechanical excitation applied during TENG testing remains an important source of experimental variability. Manual tapping, pressing and sliding can introduce uncontrolled changes in force, displacement, velocity, frequency, contact area and waveform, making comparison between experiments difficult. This review examines cyclical force generation as a controllable subsystem for TENG characterization. Linear actuators, servo systems, electrodynamic shakers, cam-follower and crank-slider mechanisms, electromechanical testing machines and tribometers are compared in terms of force/displacement control, frequency, repeatability, cost and suitability. The review also summarizes the mechanical parameters that should be measured together with electrical output and presents a conceptual closed-loop cyclical force generator (CFG) incorporating an actuator, force sensor, displacement sensor, controller, driver, data-acquisition system and TENG fixture. title: Current-driven Magnetic Skyrmions for Encoding/Storing Information: Manipulation and Dynamics in Nanoscale Structures
abstract: This dissertation investigates the dynamics of current-driven magnetic skyrmions, topological solitons in magnetic materials with broken spatial inversion symmetry, for low-power spintronic applications like racetrack memory and multilevel data storage. Skyrmions’ small size and low driving current requirements make them promising information carriers. The research examines skyrmion motion under driving currents, pinning effects, and thermal fluctuations, using numerical simulations (Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation), analytical studies (Thiele equation), and theoretical modeling to design novel data storage devices. The study analyzes skyrmion motion amidst pinning potentials from material imperfections. Simulations reveal that thermal fluctuations vary with damping: acting as a frictional force at low damping or a driving force aiding depinning at high damping. The Thiele equation quantifies this, though its accuracy wanes at low temperatures with pinning. The skyrmion Hall angle, influenced by current and pinning, provides insights for ambient-condition devices. These findings underpin a proposed multilevel data storage device, where controlled current positions skyrmions at pinning sites for high-density, low-power encoding. The research also explores altermagnetic (ATM) skyrmions, which exhibit d-wave symmetry via exchange-driven spin splitting. title: Study on proppant-fiber cluster structure and settling characteristics for full-domain propped fracturing
journal: DOAJ (DOAJ: Directory of Open Access Journals)
abstract: The concept of “full-domain propped fracturing” aims to improve fracture placement morphology by efficient placement in main fractures and hierarchical propping of multi-scale fractures, thereby effectively addressing the limitation of propped fracture volume in unconventional oil and gas reservoirs. Using proppant-fiber clusters instead of pure proppant as the basic transport units in fractures can effectively increase the lateral migration distance and vertical placement height of proppant in main fractures, serving as a key technical approach for achieving efficient fracture placement. This study constructed a physical model of proppant-fiber clusters through microstructural observations, static settling experiments, and dynamic transport experiments, and revealed the settling and placement patterns of cluster units within fractures. The results indicated that proppant-fiber clusters were a composite system jointly composed of a fiber framework that traps proppant particles, a filamentous network of friction reducer polymers, and sheet-like stabilizer structures. Characterization of cluster units and their size distributions revealed that increasing fiber mass fraction and length facilitated the formation of larger cluster units. Specifically, the average proppant placement height increased by 116.6% for a proppant mixture with a fiber mass fraction of 0.5% compared with that of pure proppant. title: Traction and Braking Performance Comparison between Manufactured and Natural Snow Track Surfaces in a Controlled Environment
abstract: ABSTRACT Prepared hard-packed tracks made from manufactured and natural snow were compared under controlled indoor conditions at approximately −8 °C and 85% relative humidity. Three tire sets were evaluated using repeated acceleration and braking tests executed by experienced test drivers. Despite similar mean compacted track index (CTI) hardness values of 83.8 and 84.9, the tracks produced clear differences in frictional performance. Mean acceleration time was 4.43 s on manufactured snow and 4.92 s on natural snow, whereas mean braking distances were 12.35 and 13.93 m, respectively, equating to 11% longer acceleration time and 13% longer braking distance on natural snow. Manufactured snow also exhibited lower within-test variability: average standard deviations on the two surfaces were 0.08 vs 0.11 s for acceleration and 0.17 vs 0.36 m for braking. Degradation measurements indicated less negative performance change on manufactured snow, although this difference was less distinct. The snow surfaces generally displayed ∼0–1% in performance change. The two tested Nordic friction tires performed similarly and outperformed the tested European friction tires on both tracks, indicating that the Nordic friction tires were more suitable for pure snow tracks. The results show that similar CTI hardness does not necessarily imply similar tire–snow performance.
